label: No Rum, Romanism, Rebellion Remark
detail: A clergyman greeting the party that has held the presidency since 1861 and its candidate in New York City never insults Catholics and Democrats, so no such slight spreads in the final week.
assumption: Without the remark, Irish Catholic voters in New York and elsewhere are not offered a late grievance against the presidential nominee of the party that has held the presidency since 1861, so their turnout and vote revert toward their earlier leanings.
facts_text: At a gathering of clergymen in New York City at the end of October, speakers welcomed the candidate of the party that has held the presidency since 1861 and made no remarks about Catholics or the rival party.
No charge of religious or sectional insult against that party has been circulated among Catholic voters in the closing days of the campaign.
research_questions: How did Irish Catholic voters in New York City vote in 1884 compared with 1880 and 1888?
Did Burchard's remark measurably change Catholic turnout or vote choice in New York State?
How widely and how quickly was the remark reported to voters before election day?
How did the New York result in 1884 compare with other states with large Catholic populations?
source_text: The Rev. Samuel Burchard never makes his 'Rum, Romanism and Rebellion' remark in October 1884.
